title: Islam: good character
hookLine: Muslims honor the Prophet's gentleness, and a hadith says the best of you are the best in character (Bukhari)

cards: The mosque in Medina, the Prophet's own. His companions sit around him. A desert traveler wanders in, a Bedouin who doesn't know the customs, walks to a corner, and starts to relieve himself on the floor.
The companions leap up, shouting, ready to drag him out. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops them. Let him finish, he says.
Then he has a bucket of water poured over the spot, calls the man over, and explains, kindly, what a mosque is for.

teach.b: That story is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and in one version the Prophet tells his companions: you were sent to make things easy, not to make them difficult. It's one of many.
The hadith collections remember his gentleness: mending his own shoes, helping at home, playing with children, standing up when a funeral passed.

teach.h: THOU ART OF A TREMENDOUS NATURE.
teach.b: The Qur'an says to him, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature."
The Arabic word there is khuluq, character, from the same family as akhlaq, the Muslim word for ethics and good conduct.
When his wife Aisha was later asked what his character was like, she answered, in a report in Sahih Muslim: his character was the Qur'an. He lived what he recited. And he set character very high.
In a hadith in Bukhari, he says: the best of you are those who are best in character.
Another says nothing will be heavier on the scale on the Day of Judgment than good character.
And another, reported in several collections, has him describe his whole mission as coming to perfect good character. So in Islam, character isn't a pleasant extra added to prayer and fasting.
It's what prayer and fasting are for. Tomorrow, that idea reaches even the fast. The Bedouin learned more from the bucket of water than from any shout.

how: Muslims study akhlaq, Islamic ethics, alongside prayer and law, and many learn the Prophet's example of gentleness from the hadith collections and biographies taught in mosques and families.

games.q: a stranger is misbehaving in the mosque, and your friends leap up to drag him out. you're the Prophet. what do you do?
o: stop them: let him finish, then clean up and explain kindly.
games.why: in Sahih al-Bukhari he stops them, has water poured, and teaches the man gently: make things easy, not difficult.

practice: Recall a moment when someone did something wrong in front of you and you wanted to shout. Replay it, and this time picture the pause: let him finish.
Then picture the bucket of water, the practical fix and the kind explanation, and let the gentler version settle in.

wordCard.voice: Islam, through good character: akhlaq, the gentleness Muslims honor in the Prophet. The best of you are the best in character. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: character, ethics; plural of khuluq.

carryVoice: Your line: best in character. Easy, not difficult: that was the Medina way. Day two hundred seventy-two, done.
